starter.plainStart: Start with one idea instead of memorizing everything at once: Newton’s third-law forces act on different objects, so they do not cancel on one object’s free-body diagram.

reasoningSteps: Define the synthetic system and observable: A level track; 20 N already denotes the sum of all horizontal forces, not a motor specification. Interpret the input tuple (10, 20) in the sequence of variables of a=F_net/m.
Derive from the governing relationship a=F_net/m. State the coordinate sign, SI dimensions and why the assumptions permit this expression rather than an unrelated formula.

Numerical result, calculated from the supplied inputs: 2 m/s². Independent algebraic or dimensional reconstruction: F_net=m*a. Reinsert this result in the inverse equation instead of relying on plausible-looking units.

Controlled sensitivity: multiply only the FIRST input in (10, 20) by 2, keeping the others fixed. Under the SAME model the predicted result becomes 1 m/s²; reason from the law whether the dependence is linear, inverse, nonlinear or sign-sensitive. A separate +1% perturbation of that same input predicts 1.980198 m/s²; this is mathematical sensitivity, not an experimentally established uncertainty budget.

Attempt falsification with a tempting false inference: The 20 N force does not imply a constant 2 m/s speed; acceleration changes velocity. Identify a measurement or sign/unit residual that would refute this claim; never use the model's numerical agreement as proof the physical assumptions are true.

Validity and evidence boundary: only net force in an inertial frame for a constant-mass body; unmodeled resistance changes F_net. Trace the mathematical statement to OpenStax University Physics Volume 1: https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-1/pages/5-3-newtons-second-law; synthetic data and counterfactuals are illustrations, not experimental measurements.

reasoningSteps: Take an ideal 2 kg object resting on a horizontal support with g=10 m/s squared. Its weight is 20 N downward and the support force is 20 N upward.
Those two forces balance on the same object. Their equality follows from zero vertical acceleration, not from their being a third-law pair.
The reaction to the support's upward force acts downward on the support. The reaction to Earth's downward gravitational force acts upward on Earth.
Label every force with both its source and its receiver. Third-law partners exchange those labels and act on different bodies, while equilibrium sums forces acting on one selected body.

reasoningSteps: Two touching blocks of masses 3 kg and 2 kg move together on an ideal frictionless horizontal surface under a 20 N push. Their common acceleration is 4 m/s squared.
When the push acts on the 3 kg block toward the 2 kg block, contact must supply the 2 kg block's acceleration, so the contact force magnitude is 8 N.
When the geometry and push direction are reversed so the 2 kg block pushes the 3 kg block, the contact force magnitude is 12 N, even though the system acceleration magnitude remains 4 m/s squared.
In each arrangement, the two contact forces are equal and opposite on different blocks. They cancel only when summing the two-block system; the external 20 N push does not cancel.
Reference: https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-1/pages/5-5-newtons-third-law . These are original synthetic Newtonian calculations under explicit ideal assumptions.

reasoningSteps: For an ideal 2 kg object accelerating vertically with its support, take upward as positive and g=10 m/s squared. The force equation is N-mg=ma.
At upward acceleration 2 m/s squared, N=24 N. At downward acceleration 2 m/s squared, a=-2 and N=16 N.
At a=-10 m/s squared, the model reaches free fall and N=0, while gravitational weight remains 20 N.
A simple support cannot pull the object downward. A proposed acceleration below -g would make the contact formula demand negative N, signaling loss of contact rather than a negative scale reading.
Reference: https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-1/pages/5-5-newtons-third-law . These are original synthetic Newtonian calculations under explicit ideal assumptions.

vocabulary.term: Newton’s Laws as a Model of Motion

vocabulary.term: Electric Fields: Force Per Unit Charge
vocabulary.definition: An electric field describes the force a positive test charge would experience per unit charge at a point in space.

vocabulary.term: Torque: The Rotational Effect of Force
vocabulary.definition: Torque measures how strongly a force tends to rotate an object about an axis or pivot.

vocabulary.term: Newtonian Gravity
vocabulary.definition: Newtonian gravitation models the attractive force between two point masses as proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of their separation.

vocabulary.term: Magnetic Force on a Moving Charge
vocabulary.definition: A magnetic field exerts a force q v × B on a charge moving with velocity v.

vocabulary.term: Coulomb Force
vocabulary.definition: The magnitude of the electrostatic force between two point charges is proportional to the product of their charges and inversely proportional to the square of their separation.

reasoningSteps: Use a synthetic 5 kg block on a horizontal surface, g=10 m/s squared, coefficient of static friction 0.4 and coefficient of kinetic friction 0.3. With no other vertical force, N=50 N.
The maximum static friction is 20 N. A 12 N horizontal push on the initially resting block requires only 12 N of opposing static friction, so acceleration is zero.
At the ideal threshold of 20 N, static balance can still be possible. A 25 N push exceeds the static limit, so the resting no-slip assumption fails.

While sliding in the push direction under the stated kinetic-friction model, friction is 15 N and acceleration is (25-15)/5=2 m/s squared. Static and kinetic laws describe different regimes; do not apply a fixed kinetic-friction direction after motion stops or reverses.
Reference: https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-1/pages/6-2-friction . These are original synthetic Newtonian calculations under explicit ideal assumptions.
